Chapter 4 — Local Methods: k-Nearest Neighbors and the Bias–Variance Trade-off

How can a method with no model at all, which just looks at the closest examples it has seen, work so well? And what does its one knob, the number of neighbors, teach us about every other learning method?

4.1 Learning objectives¶

Chapter 3 showed that learning is possible when the class of functions is not too rich, and that the price of richness is a gap between training and test error. This chapter makes that statement concrete with the simplest learning method there is. The k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) method has no training phase and no parameters to fit: to predict at a new point it looks at the kkk closest training points and averages their labels. Despite its simplicity it is a serious method (it is still used, and it is hard to beat on some problems), it is completely analyzable, and its single hyperparameter kkk moves smoothly from a very flexible model (k=1k = 1k=1) to a very rigid one (k=nk = nk=n). That makes it the ideal laboratory for the bias–variance trade-off, the idea that organizes the whole of Part II.

After working through this chapter you will be able to:

  1. write the k-NN classifier and k-NN regressor, implement them from scratch with the vectorized distances of Chapter 2, and check your code against scikit-learn;

  2. explain how kkk controls the flexibility of the decision boundary and of the fitted curve, and why the training error can never be used to choose it;

  3. derive the bias–variance decomposition of the squared error, and use it to compute exactly the bias and the variance of k-NN regression;

  4. explain, and verify by experiment, why the best kkk grows with the sample size while the neighborhoods shrink;

  5. state the Cover–Hart theorem (the 1-NN error is at most twice the Bayes error) and the consistency of k-NN when k→∞k \to \inftyk→∞ and k/n→0k/n \to 0k/n→0;

  6. describe the curse of dimensionality in three ways (empty neighborhoods, concentration of distances, slow rates), measure it on real data, and say what helps;

  7. choose a distance and a weighting scheme sensibly, and explain when tree-based neighbor search (KD-trees, ball trees) is faster than brute force and when it is not.

Prerequisites. Chapters 1 to 3. In particular the vectorized distances of Worked example 2.1 and Exercise 2.7, the standardization of Section 2.7, and the Bayes predictor and the approximation–estimation split of Sections 3.2 and 3.3.

A word about the data in this chapter

The experiments use real data sets that ship with scikit-learn: Digits (images of handwritten digits), Wine, Diabetes and Breast Cancer. To check the bias–variance formulas exactly we need a world in which the true function is known, so Sections 4.5 and 4.6 and part of Section 4.7 use simulated data. Whenever that is the case, the text says so.

4.2 The nearest-neighbor idea¶

4.2.1 The method¶

Let S={(xi,yi)}i=1nS = \{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}S={(xi​,yi​)}i=1n​ be the training set and let x\mathbf{x}x be a new input. Measure the distance from x\mathbf{x}x to every training input, usually the Euclidean distance ∥x−xi∥2\lVert \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_i\rVert_2∥x−xi​∥2​, and call Nk(x)N_k(\mathbf{x})Nk​(x) the set of the kkk training points closest to x\mathbf{x}x (the kkk nearest neighbors). The prediction is built from the labels of these points only:

f^k(x)=1k∑i∈Nk(x)yi(regression),f^k(x)=argmax⁡c ∑i∈Nk(x)I[yi=c](classification).\hat f_{k}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i \in N_k(\mathbf{x})} y_i \quad\text{(regression)}, \qquad\qquad \hat f_{k}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname*{argmax}_{c}\ \sum_{i \in N_k(\mathbf{x})} \mathbb{I}[y_i = c] \quad\text{(classification)}.f^​k​(x)=k1​i∈Nk​(x)∑​yi​(regression),f^​k​(x)=cargmax​ i∈Nk​(x)∑​I[yi​=c](classification).
(1)

For regression we average the neighbors’ targets; for classification we take a majority vote. That is the whole method. A few observations will be useful later.

  • There is nothing to train. The “model” is the training set itself, which is why k-NN is called a memory-based or instance-based method. All the work happens at prediction time, and a prediction costs a distance computation to each of the nnn training points, O(nd)O(nd)O(nd) operations (Section 4.8 discusses how to do better).

  • It is a local method. The prediction at x\mathbf{x}x depends only on the training points near x\mathbf{x}x. A flexible global function is replaced by many small local decisions.

  • It assumes that closeness means similarity: points that are close in feature space have similar labels. This is its inductive bias in the sense of Section 3.9 (it is in the table there), and everything that follows, including the curse of dimensionality, is a consequence of when this assumption holds and when it fails.

  • Ties can occur in a vote (for kkk even, or with several classes). Common rules are to take the class of the single nearest neighbor among the tied ones, or the smallest label. For two classes an odd kkk avoids ties.

  • The value k=1k = 1k=1 gives zero error on the training set (each training point is its own nearest neighbor, assuming no two identical inputs have different labels), and k=nk = nk=n predicts the global mean, or the majority class, for every input. Between these extremes kkk is a hyperparameter in the sense of Chapter 1.

4.2.2 An implementation from scratch, and handwritten digits¶

The data set for this section is Digits: 1,797 grayscale images of handwritten digits 0 to 9, each of 8×88 \times 88×8 pixels with intensities from 0 to 16, flattened into a vector of d=64d = 64d=64 features. It is a small relative of the famous MNIST data set (60,000 images of 28×2828 \times 2828×28 pixels) and is a classical test bed for nearest-neighbor methods.

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

digits = load_digits()
X_dg, y_dg = digits.data, digits.target
print("shape of X:", X_dg.shape, "| pixel values from", X_dg.min(), "to", X_dg.max())
print("images per class:", np.bincount(y_dg))

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X_dg, y_dg, test_size=0.3, random_state=SEED, stratify=y_dg)
print("training set:", X_tr.shape, "| test set:", X_te.shape)
shape of X: (1797, 64) | pixel values from 0.0 to 16.0
images per class: [178 182 177 183 181 182 181 179 174 180]
training set: (1257, 64) | test set: (540, 64)

We write the classifier with the Gram-matrix identity of Worked example 2.1, so that all the distances between the test points and the training points are computed at once, with no Python loop over the samples. The function np.argpartition finds the indices of the kkk smallest entries of each row without sorting the whole row, and a vectorized bincount counts the votes.

def knn_predict(X_train, y_train, X_test, k):
    """k-NN classifier with the Euclidean distance. Ties go to the smallest class label."""
    sq_train = (X_train ** 2).sum(axis=1)
    sq_test = (X_test ** 2).sum(axis=1)
    D2 = sq_test[:, None] + sq_train[None, :] - 2 * X_test @ X_train.T        # (n_test, n_train) squared distances
    nearest = np.argpartition(D2, kth=k - 1, axis=1)[:, :k]                   # indices of the k nearest, in no particular order
    votes = y_train[nearest]                                                  # (n_test, k) labels of the neighbors
    n_classes = y_train.max() + 1
    counts = np.apply_along_axis(np.bincount, 1, votes, minlength=n_classes)  # (n_test, n_classes) vote counts
    return counts.argmax(axis=1)


from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

for k in (1, 5, 15):
    ours = knn_predict(X_tr, y_tr, X_te, k)
    theirs = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k).fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict(X_te)
    print(f"k = {k:>2}: test accuracy {np.mean(ours == y_te):.4f} (ours) | {np.mean(theirs == y_te):.4f} (scikit-learn) "
          f"| the two agree on {np.mean(ours == theirs):.4f} of the test images")
k =  1: test accuracy 0.9870 (ours) | 0.9870 (scikit-learn) | the two agree on 1.0000 of the test images
k =  5: test accuracy 0.9870 (ours) | 0.9870 (scikit-learn) | the two agree on 1.0000 of the test images

k = 15: test accuracy 0.9722 (ours) | 0.9722 (scikit-learn) | the two agree on 1.0000 of the test images

The two implementations agree on practically every image (they can differ only when several training points are at exactly the same distance from the test point, and then they break the tie in different ways). Accuracy above 98% from a method with no training at all is striking. Where does it come from, and where does it fail? Figure 4.1 shows the five nearest neighbors of five test digits: three that the classifier gets right and two that it gets wrong.

# Figure 4.1 — the five nearest neighbors of some test digits
def figure_4_1():
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    pred = knn.predict(X_te)
    wrong = np.flatnonzero(pred != y_te)
    right = np.flatnonzero(pred == y_te)
    chosen = list(right[:3]) + list(wrong[:2])

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(6, 5, figsize=(6.4, 8.0))
    for col, i in enumerate(chosen):
        neighbors = knn.kneighbors(X_te[i:i + 1], return_distance=False)[0]
        axes[0, col].imshow(X_te[i].reshape(8, 8), cmap="gray_r")
        color = "black" if pred[i] == y_te[i] else VERMILION
        axes[0, col].set_title(f"true {y_te[i]}, pred. {pred[i]}", fontsize=9.5, color=color)
        for row, j in enumerate(neighbors, start=1):
            axes[row, col].imshow(X_tr[j].reshape(8, 8), cmap="gray_r")
            axes[row, col].set_title(f"label {y_tr[j]}", fontsize=9, color=("black" if y_tr[j] == y_te[i] else VERMILION))
    for ax in axes.ravel():
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
    axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("test", fontsize=9)
    for row in range(1, 6):
        axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(f"#{row}", fontsize=9)
    fig.suptitle("A test digit (top) and its five nearest training digits", fontsize=11)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_4_1()

In the three successful cases all five neighbors have the right label: the test digit sits in the middle of a cluster of similar images. In the two failures all five neighbors agree and are all wrong: the test digit (a 5 drawn like a 9, an 8 drawn as a thin vertical stroke) is simply closer to the examples of another class than to the other examples of its own. This is the noise floor R∗R^\astR∗ of Section 3.2 in action: no method that only sees these 64 numbers can do much better on such images.

Worked example 4.1 — k-NN by hand¶

Six labeled points in the plane: class ∘ at A=(0,0)A = (0, 0)A=(0,0), B=(1,0)B = (1, 0)B=(1,0), C=(0,1)C = (0, 1)C=(0,1) and class ∙\bullet∙ at D=(3,3)D = (3, 3)D=(3,3), E=(4,3)E = (4, 3)E=(4,3), F=(3,4)F = (3, 4)F=(3,4). Classify the new point x=(2,2)\mathbf{x} = (2, 2)x=(2,2), and then the point z=(1,1)\mathbf{z} = (1, 1)z=(1,1).

By hand. The squared distances from x=(2,2)\mathbf{x} = (2, 2)x=(2,2) are AAA: 8, BBB: 1+4=51 + 4 = 51+4=5, CCC: 4+1=54 + 1 = 54+1=5, DDD: 1+1=21 + 1 = 21+1=2, EEE: 4+1=54 + 1 = 54+1=5, FFF: 1+4=51 + 4 = 51+4=5. The nearest neighbor is DDD (∙\bullet∙), so k=1k = 1k=1 gives ∙\bullet∙. For k=3k = 3k=3 the three nearest are DDD and then four points tied at squared distance 5 (BBB, CCC, EEE, FFF): the neighbor set is not uniquely defined, and the vote depends on how the tie is broken, from ∙∙∙\bullet\bullet\bullet∙∙∙ to ∙∘∘\bullet\circ\circ∙∘∘. This is not a pathological case: with integer-valued or rounded features exact ties are common, and the implementation of the tie-breaking rule can change the result. For k=5k = 5k=5 the neighbor set is {D,B,C,E,F}\{D, B, C, E, F\}{D,B,C,E,F}, with three ∙\bullet∙ and two ∘, and the vote gives ∙\bullet∙.

For z=(1,1)\mathbf{z} = (1, 1)z=(1,1) the squared distances are AAA: 2, BBB: 1, CCC: 1, DDD: 8, EEE: 13, FFF: 13. The three nearest are BBB, CCC, AAA, all ∘, and k=1,3k = 1, 3k=1,3 give ∘. For k=5k = 5k=5 we add DDD and one of EEE, FFF (tied at 13): the vote is 3∘3 \circ3∘ against 2∙2 \bullet2∙, still ∘.

With Python. The cell below checks the distances and the votes. Note that KNeighborsClassifier returns a definite answer even for the tied case (k=3k = 3k=3 at x\mathbf{x}x, where it answers class 0, the two tied points that come first in the training set), but a different implementation could have answered differently.

P = np.array([[0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1], [3, 3], [4, 3], [3, 4]], dtype=float)
labels = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1])                   # 0 = circle, 1 = bullet
for name, q in [("x = (2, 2)", [2.0, 2.0]), ("z = (1, 1)", [1.0, 1.0])]:
    d2 = ((P - np.array(q)) ** 2).sum(axis=1)
    print(f"{name}: squared distances to A..F = {d2}")
    for k in (1, 3, 5):
        pred = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k).fit(P, labels).predict([q])[0]
        print(f"   k = {k}: predicted class {pred}")

4.3 How kkk controls flexibility¶

4.3.1 The decision boundary¶

For a classifier the effect of kkk is best seen in the plane. We take two features of the Wine data (flavanoids and color_intensity, which separate the three cultivars well but not perfectly), standardize them (Chapter 2: k-NN is distance-based, so the scales matter; the scaler is fitted on the training set only), and color the plane by the class that k-NN predicts at each point. Figure 4.2 shows four values of kkk.

from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap

wine = load_wine(as_frame=True)
features2 = ["flavanoids", "color_intensity"]
X_w2 = wine.data[features2].to_numpy()
y_w = wine.target.to_numpy()
Xw_tr, Xw_te, yw_tr, yw_te = train_test_split(X_w2, y_w, test_size=0.3, random_state=SEED, stratify=y_w)
print("training set of the figure, examples per cultivar:", np.bincount(yw_tr))


# Figure 4.2 — decision regions of k-NN for four values of k
def figure_4_2():
    ks = [1, 5, 25, 100]
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(0.2, 5.6, 300), np.linspace(1.0, 13.5, 300))
    grid = np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]
    light = ListedColormap(["#CFE4F3", "#FBE3B0", "#C4E8DD"])
    dark = [BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN]
    markers = ["o", "^", "s"]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9.2, 7.4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    for ax, k in zip(axes.ravel(), ks):
        model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)).fit(Xw_tr, yw_tr)
        ax.pcolormesh(xx, yy, model.predict(grid).reshape(xx.shape), cmap=light, shading="auto", vmin=0, vmax=2)
        for c in range(3):
            ax.scatter(*Xw_tr[yw_tr == c].T, color=dark[c], marker=markers[c], s=26, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5,
                       label=f"cultivar {c}")
        ax.set_title(f"k = {k}: training accuracy {model.score(Xw_tr, yw_tr):.2f}, test accuracy {model.score(Xw_te, yw_te):.2f}", fontsize=10.5)
        ax.grid(False)
    for ax in axes[1]:
        ax.set_xlabel("flavanoids")
    for ax in axes[:, 0]:
        ax.set_ylabel("color intensity")
    axes[0, 0].legend(frameon=True, fontsize=9, loc="upper left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_4_2()
training set of the figure, examples per cultivar: [41 50 33]

Reading the figure. With k=1k = 1k=1 the plane is divided into the Voronoi cells of the training points: every training point owns the region closer to it than to any other point, so the boundary follows the training data exactly, with islands around isolated points (training accuracy 1.00, by construction). As kkk grows the boundary smooths out, because a point must now beat several neighbors; at k=25k = 25k=25 the regions are three compact blobs. At k=100k = 100k=100 something drastic happens: the training set has only 124 points (41, 50 and 33 per cultivar), so a vote among 100 neighbors is almost a vote among everybody, cultivar 2 can never win it, and its region disappears; the test accuracy collapses to 0.41, close to the frequency of the largest class. The number of neighbors is a smoothing parameter: small kkk means a complex, wiggly boundary (low bias, high variance in the language we are about to define), large kkk a simple one (high bias, low variance).

4.3.2 The error curves, and why the training error cannot choose kkk¶

Figure 4.2 shows one split. To see the typical behavior we repeat the train/test split many times and average the accuracies, for every kkk on a grid. We do it for two data sets of very different character: Digits (all 64 pixels) and the two-feature Wine problem above. In both we also compute the accuracy on the training set.

def accuracy_curves(X, y, ks, n_repeats=20, scale=False, test_size=0.3):
    """Mean and std of the training and test accuracy of k-NN over random stratified splits."""
    tr_acc = np.zeros((n_repeats, len(ks)))
    te_acc = np.zeros((n_repeats, len(ks)))
    for r in range(n_repeats):
        Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=test_size, random_state=r, stratify=y)
        for j, k in enumerate(ks):
            model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)
            if scale:
                model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), model)
            model.fit(Xa, ya)
            tr_acc[r, j], te_acc[r, j] = model.score(Xa, ya), model.score(Xb, yb)
    return tr_acc, te_acc


ks_digits = [1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 25, 50, 100, 200]
ks_wine = [1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 60, 80, 100]
curves = {
    "digits": (ks_digits, *accuracy_curves(X_dg, y_dg, ks_digits)),
    "wine2": (ks_wine, *accuracy_curves(X_w2, y_w, ks_wine, scale=True)),
}
for name, (ks, tr_acc, te_acc) in curves.items():
    table = pd.DataFrame({"training": tr_acc.mean(axis=0), "test": te_acc.mean(axis=0), "std of test": te_acc.std(axis=0)}, index=pd.Index(ks, name="k"))
    print(f"--- {name}: mean accuracy over 20 random 70/30 splits")
    print(table.round(4).T.to_string())
    best = ks[int(te_acc.mean(axis=0).argmax())]
    print(f"best k on the test sets = {best} (test accuracy {te_acc.mean(axis=0).max():.4f}); "
          f"k chosen by the training accuracy = {ks[int(tr_acc.mean(axis=0).argmax())]}\n")

# Figure 4.3 — training and test accuracy of k-NN as a function of k
def figure_4_3():
    titles = {"digits": "(a) Digits: 64 pixels, little noise", "wine2": "(b) Wine, two features: more overlap between classes"}
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 4.2))
    for ax, (name, (ks, tr_acc, te_acc)) in zip(axes, curves.items()):
        for acc, color, marker, label in [(tr_acc, VERMILION, "o", "training accuracy"), (te_acc, BLUE, "s", "test accuracy")]:
            ax.plot(ks, acc.mean(axis=0), color=color, marker=marker, linewidth=2, label=label)
            ax.fill_between(ks, acc.mean(axis=0) - acc.std(axis=0), acc.mean(axis=0) + acc.std(axis=0), color=color, alpha=0.15)
        best = int(te_acc.mean(axis=0).argmax())
        ax.axvline(ks[best], color="gray", linestyle=":", linewidth=1.5)
        ax.annotate(f"best k = {ks[best]}", (ks[best], te_acc.mean(axis=0)[best]), xytext=(12, -34), textcoords="offset points",
                    fontsize=10, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="gray"))
        ax.set_xscale("log")
        ax.set(xlabel="number of neighbors $k$ (log scale)", ylabel="accuracy", title=titles[name])
        ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_4_3()

What the curves say.

  1. The training accuracy cannot choose kkk. It equals exactly 1.00 at k=1k = 1k=1 in both panels and falls as kkk grows, so the rule “pick the kkk with the best training accuracy” returns k=1k = 1k=1 on every problem (last line of each block of output). This is the optimism of Section 3.4 in its purest form: a 1-NN classifier memorizes the training set, and a method that memorizes is not tested by the training data. On Wine the gap between the two curves at k=1k = 1k=1 is 1.000−0.919=0.0811.000 - 0.919 = 0.0811.000−0.919=0.081; at k=15k = 15k=15 it is 0.939−0.9300.939 - 0.9300.939−0.930, about 0.01. The test set, or the validation procedures of Chapter 5, are what we use to choose.

  2. The best kkk depends on how noisy the problem is. On Digits the best kkk is 1 (0.985), and kkk up to 5 is statistically indistinguishable from it: the classes are almost separable in pixel space, so the single nearest neighbor is nearly always right and averaging several neighbors only adds a bias. On the two Wine features the classes overlap, a single neighbor is unreliable, and the test accuracy peaks at k=15k = 15k=15 (0.930), although everything from k=1k = 1k=1 to k=20k = 20k=20 lies within one standard deviation of it. The numbers of this experiment cannot resolve a finer choice; the message is that there is a wide plateau, and that the plateau is wider and shifts to larger kkk when the data are noisier.

  3. Too large a kkk underfits. Past the plateau both curves fall together (the gap between training and test accuracy vanishes, because the model has become too simple to depend on the particular sample): Digits drops to 0.880 at k=200k = 200k=200, Wine to 0.415 at k=100k = 100k=100, where the vote reports little more than the class frequencies.

Chapter 3 described this picture in general terms (Figure 3.3): a flexible model has a large estimation error, a rigid one a large approximation error. The next sections make it precise for the squared loss, where the trade-off becomes an exact formula.

4.4 k-NN for regression¶

For a numeric target the prediction is the average of the targets of the kkk nearest neighbors, f^k(x)=1k∑i∈Nk(x)yi\hat f_k(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\in N_k(\mathbf{x})} y_if^​k​(x)=k1​∑i∈Nk​(x)​yi​. It is a local average, the simplest example of a nonparametric estimator of the regression function η(x)=E[y∣x]\eta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[y\mid\mathbf{x}]η(x)=E[y∣x] of Section 3.2: it makes no assumption about the shape of η\etaη beyond “similar inputs have similar targets”. The result is a piecewise-constant function, which jumps whenever the set of neighbors changes.

We use the Diabetes data (442 patients, ten baseline measurements, and a numeric measure of disease progression one year later, which we will call the progression). Starting with one feature makes the fitted function visible: Figure 4.4 shows the progression against the body-mass index (bmi), with the k-NN fit for four values of kkk and, for comparison, the least-squares line.

from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

diabetes = load_diabetes(as_frame=True)
X_db = diabetes.data.to_numpy()
y_db = diabetes.target.to_numpy()
feature_names = list(diabetes.data.columns)
bmi = X_db[:, [feature_names.index("bmi")]]
print("patients:", len(y_db), "| features:", feature_names)
print("each feature is already centered, with the same scale: column std", X_db.std(axis=0).round(3)[:3], "...")


# Figure 4.4 — k-NN regression of the progression on bmi, for four values of k
def figure_4_4():
    grid = np.linspace(bmi.min(), bmi.max(), 600)[:, None]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 4.4), sharey=True)
    for ax, ks, colors in [(axes[0], [1, 10], [VERMILION, BLUE]), (axes[1], [40, 160], [BLUE, VERMILION])]:
        ax.scatter(bmi, y_db, s=14, color="gray", alpha=0.45, label="patients")
        for k, color, ls in zip(ks, colors, ["-", "--"]):
            ax.plot(grid, KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=k).fit(bmi, y_db).predict(grid), color=color, linestyle=ls, linewidth=2.2, label=f"k-NN, k = {k}")
        ax.plot(grid, LinearRegression().fit(bmi, y_db).predict(grid), color=GREEN, linestyle=":", linewidth=2.2, label="least squares line")
        ax.set(xlabel="body-mass index (centered and scaled by scikit-learn)", title=f"k = {ks[0]} and k = {ks[1]}")
        ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left", fontsize=9.5)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("disease progression")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_4_4()
patients: 442 | features: ['age', 'sex', 'bmi', 'bp', 's1', 's2', 's3', 's4', 's5', 's6']
each feature is already centered, with the same scale: column std [0.048 0.048 0.048] ...

The same picture as in the classification case: k=1k = 1k=1 passes through every point and jumps wildly (it fits the noise); k=10k = 10k=10 is still rough; k=40k = 40k=40 follows a smooth, nearly linear trend that bends slightly at the extremes; k=160k = 160k=160, a vote among more than a third of the patients, flattens the curve and loses the trend at both ends (a bias toward the global mean). Note also that at the edges of the xxx-range all neighbors lie on one side of the query point, which pulls the average toward the interior: the boundary effect, which will matter in the next section.

How accurate are these fits? We measure the mean squared error (MSE) on held-out patients, averaged over 20 random 70/30 splits, for kkk from 1 to 160, using the single feature bmi and then all ten features, and compare with linear regression on the same inputs. (Chapter 5 will present better ways to do this; here repeated splits are enough.)

def regression_mse(features, ks, n_repeats=20):
    """Mean test MSE of k-NN regression for each k, and of least squares, over random 70/30 splits."""
    mse_knn = np.zeros((n_repeats, len(ks)))
    mse_lin = np.zeros(n_repeats)
    for r in range(n_repeats):
        Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(X_db[:, features], y_db, test_size=0.3, random_state=r)
        for j, k in enumerate(ks):
            mse_knn[r, j] = np.mean((KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=k).fit(Xa, ya).predict(Xb) - yb) ** 2)
        mse_lin[r] = np.mean((LinearRegression().fit(Xa, ya).predict(Xb) - yb) ** 2)
    return mse_knn.mean(axis=0), mse_lin.mean()


ks_reg = [1, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160]
rows = {}
for name, cols in [("bmi only", [feature_names.index("bmi")]), ("all 10 features", list(range(10)))]:
    mse_knn, mse_lin = regression_mse(cols, ks_reg)
    rows[name] = {**{f"k = {k}": v for k, v in zip(ks_reg, mse_knn)}, "least squares": mse_lin}
print(f"variance of the target (the MSE of always predicting the mean): {y_db.var():.0f}\n")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(0).astype(int).to_string())
variance of the target (the MSE of always predicting the mean): 5930

                 k = 1  k = 5  k = 10  k = 20  k = 40  k = 80  k = 160  least squares
bmi only          7419   4508    4162    4033    3965    4003     4262           3801
all 10 features   6208   3682    3365    3283    3371    3531     4089           3016

Three lessons. First, the same U-shape of Chapter 1 appears: with bmi alone the error falls from 7,621 at k=1k = 1k=1 to a minimum near k=40k = 40k=40 and rises again at k=160k = 160k=160, and for all ten features the best value is k=20k = 20k=20. Second, k=1k = 1k=1 is much worse than predicting the mean (variance of the target 5,930), the most visible symptom of fitting the noise. Third, and this is important to say, k-NN does not win here: least squares is better than the best k-NN, in both settings. The reason is again the inductive bias of Section 3.9. The relation between these ten measurements and the progression is close to linear, and a model that assumes linearity uses all 309 training patients to estimate a handful of coefficients, while k-NN, which assumes only smoothness, averages over a few dozen neighbors in a ten-dimensional space where neighbors are not very close (Section 4.7). A more flexible method is better only when the truth requires the flexibility, or when there is enough data to pay for it.

4.5 The bias–variance decomposition¶

4.5.1 The squared error at a point, split in three¶

Consider a fixed input x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​. The target there is y0=f(x0)+εy_0 = f(\mathbf{x}_0) + \varepsilony0​=f(x0​)+ε, where f(x0)=E[y0∣x0]f(\mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbb{E}[y_0\mid\mathbf{x}_0]f(x0​)=E[y0​∣x0​] is the regression function η\etaη of Chapter 3 (we write fff for the true function from now on) and the noise ε\varepsilonε has mean 0 and variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, independent of everything else. We train a method on a random training set SSS and get the prediction f^S(x0)\hat f_S(\mathbf{x}_0)f^​S​(x0​), which is itself a random variable because SSS is random. The expected squared error at x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​, averaged over the noise of the new target and over the training set, splits into three non-negative pieces:

  E[(y0−f^S(x0))2]=σ2⏟noise+(f(x0)−E[f^S(x0)])2⏟bias2+E[(f^S(x0)−E[f^S(x0)])2]⏟variance  \boxed{\;\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(y_0 - \hat f_S(\mathbf{x}_0)\big)^2\Big] = \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{noise}} + \underbrace{\big(f(\mathbf{x}_0) - \mathbb{E}[\hat f_S(\mathbf{x}_0)]\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(\hat f_S(\mathbf{x}_0) - \mathbb{E}[\hat f_S(\mathbf{x}_0)]\big)^2\Big]}_{\text{variance}}\;}E[(y0​−f^​S​(x0​))2]=noiseσ2​​+bias2(f(x0​)−E[f^​S​(x0​)])2​​+varianceE[(f^​S​(x0​)−E[f^​S​(x0​)])2]​​​
(2)
Proof

Write fˉ=E[f^S(x0)]\bar f = \mathbb{E}[\hat f_S(\mathbf{x}_0)]fˉ​=E[f^​S​(x0​)] for the average prediction over training sets, and add and subtract f(x0)f(\mathbf{x}_0)f(x0​) and fˉ\bar ffˉ​:

y0−f^S=(y0−f)⏟ε+(f−fˉ)⏟a constant+(fˉ−f^S)⏟mean zero.y_0 - \hat f_S = \underbrace{(y_0 - f)}_{\varepsilon} + \underbrace{(f - \bar f)}_{\text{a constant}} + \underbrace{(\bar f - \hat f_S)}_{\text{mean zero}} .y0​−f^​S​=ε(y0​−f)​​+a constant(f−fˉ​)​​+mean zero(fˉ​−f^​S​)​​.
(3)

Square the sum. The three squares give σ2\sigma^2σ2, (f−fˉ)2(f - \bar f)^2(f−fˉ​)2 and Var⁡(f^S)\operatorname{Var}(\hat f_S)Var(f^​S​). The cross terms vanish: E[ε (f−fˉ)]=0\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\,(f - \bar f)] = 0E[ε(f−fˉ​)]=0 because ε\varepsilonε has mean 0 and f−fˉf - \bar ff−fˉ​ is a constant; E[ε (fˉ−f^S)]=0\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\,(\bar f - \hat f_S)] = 0E[ε(fˉ​−f^​S​)]=0 because ε\varepsilonε (the noise in the new target) is independent of the training set; and E[(f−fˉ)(fˉ−f^S)]=(f−fˉ) E[fˉ−f^S]=0\mathbb{E}[(f - \bar f)(\bar f - \hat f_S)] = (f - \bar f)\,\mathbb{E}[\bar f - \hat f_S] = 0E[(f−fˉ​)(fˉ​−f^​S​)]=(f−fˉ​)E[fˉ​−f^​S​]=0. □\square□

  • The noise σ2\sigma^2σ2 is the part of the target that no function of x\mathbf{x}x can predict: it is the Bayes risk R∗R^\astR∗ of Section 3.2 (for the squared loss, the conditional variance, here constant). It does not depend on the method.

  • The bias measures a systematic error: how far the average prediction, over many hypothetical training sets, is from the truth. A method with a high bias is too rigid to represent fff.

  • The variance measures sensitivity to the sample: how much the prediction at x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​ would change if we drew another training set of the same size. A method with a high variance reacts to the idiosyncrasies of the sample, i.e. to its noise.

Averaging over x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​ gives the expected risk of Chapter 3: ES[R(f^S)]=R∗+bias2‾+variance‾\mathbb{E}_S[R(\hat f_S)] = R^\ast + \overline{\text{bias}^2} + \overline{\text{variance}}ES​[R(f^​S​)]=R∗+bias2+variance. This is a close cousin of the split of Section 3.3 into approximation and estimation error, and it is easy to confuse the two. In Chapter 3 the approximation error was a property of the class H\mathcal{H}H (the distance between its best member and the truth), and the estimation error the extra price for choosing a member from a finite sample. Here bias and variance are properties of the algorithm at a given sample size; bias is the average distance to the truth of the function the algorithm returns (which includes the approximation error, and also the systematic effect of how it chooses within the class), and variance is the randomness of that function. For a rich class and plenty of data they are nearly the same thing, and in both pictures the message is the same: flexibility reduces bias and increases variance.

Pitfall — the decomposition is for the squared loss

The three terms add up exactly only for the squared loss. For the 0–1 loss of classification the error does not split additively, and several different “bias–variance decompositions” have been proposed, none with all the nice properties. The qualitative picture (a flexible classifier has a high variance, a rigid one a high bias) remains true, and Figures 4.2 and 4.3 are its illustration.

4.5.2 The decomposition of k-NN regression, in closed form¶

For k-NN regression the three terms can be computed explicitly if we make the simplest assumption on how the training inputs are generated: the fixed design, in which the inputs x1,…,xn\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_nx1​,…,xn​ are fixed numbers and only the targets yi=f(xi)+εiy_i = f(\mathbf{x}_i) + \varepsilon_iyi​=f(xi​)+εi​ are random, with independent noises of variance σ2\sigma^2σ2. (This is the standard setting of the theory of regression, and it makes the neighbor set Nk(x0)N_k(\mathbf{x}_0)Nk​(x0​) non-random, which is what makes an exact computation possible.) The prediction is f^k(x0)=1k∑i∈Nk(x0)(f(xi)+εi)\hat f_k(\mathbf{x}_0) = \frac1k\sum_{i\in N_k(\mathbf{x}_0)}\big(f(\mathbf{x}_i) + \varepsilon_i\big)f^​k​(x0​)=k1​∑i∈Nk​(x0​)​(f(xi​)+εi​), and therefore

E[f^k(x0)]=1k∑i∈Nk(x0)f(xi),Var⁡[f^k(x0)]=1k2∑i∈Nk(x0)σ2=σ2k.\mathbb{E}\big[\hat f_k(\mathbf{x}_0)\big] = \frac1k\sum_{i\in N_k(\mathbf{x}_0)} f(\mathbf{x}_i), \qquad \operatorname{Var}\big[\hat f_k(\mathbf{x}_0)\big] = \frac{1}{k^2}\sum_{i\in N_k(\mathbf{x}_0)}\sigma^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{k}.E[f^​k​(x0​)]=k1​i∈Nk​(x0​)∑​f(xi​),Var[f^​k​(x0​)]=k21​i∈Nk​(x0​)∑​σ2=kσ2​.
(4)

(The variance of a sum of independent variables is the sum of the variances; the factor 1/k21/k^21/k2 comes from the average.) The expected squared error at x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​ is thus

  E[(y0−f^k(x0))2]=σ2+(f(x0)−1k∑i∈Nk(x0)f(xi))2+σ2k  \boxed{\;\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(y_0 - \hat f_k(\mathbf{x}_0)\big)^2\Big] = \sigma^2 + \Big(f(\mathbf{x}_0) - \frac1k\sum_{i\in N_k(\mathbf{x}_0)} f(\mathbf{x}_i)\Big)^2 + \frac{\sigma^2}{k}\;}E[(y0​−f^​k​(x0​))2]=σ2+(f(x0​)−k1​i∈Nk​(x0​)∑​f(xi​))2+kσ2​​
(5)

Everything is now visible. The variance is σ2/k\sigma^2/kσ2/k: it decreases like 1/k1/k1/k, because we average more noisy numbers, and for k=1k = 1k=1 it equals the noise itself, so that 1-NN doubles the unavoidable error (σ2+σ2\sigma^2 + \sigma^2σ2+σ2, if the bias is negligible). The bias is the difference between the true value at x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​ and the average of the true values at the neighbors; it grows with kkk because the neighbors that are added are farther away, where fff differs more from f(x0)f(\mathbf{x}_0)f(x0​).

Worked example 4.2 — bias and variance by hand¶

Let f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2 and σ2=0.25\sigma^2 = 0.25σ2=0.25, with the training inputs x=0,1,2,3,4x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4x=0,1,2,3,4 (so that f=0,1,4,9,16f = 0, 1, 4, 9, 16f=0,1,4,9,16). Take x0=2x_0 = 2x0​=2 (a point of the design, in the interior).

By hand. For k=1k = 1k=1: N1={2}N_1 = \{2\}N1​={2}, the average of fff over the neighbors is 4=f(x0)4 = f(x_0)4=f(x0​), so the bias is 0 and the variance is 0.25; total 0.25+0+0.25=0.500.25 + 0 + 0.25 = 0.500.25+0+0.25=0.50. For k=3k = 3k=3: N3={1,2,3}N_3 = \{1, 2, 3\}N3​={1,2,3}, average (1+4+9)/3=14/3=4.667(1 + 4 + 9)/3 = 14/3 = 4.667(1+4+9)/3=14/3=4.667, bias =4−4.667=−0.667= 4 - 4.667 = -0.667=4−4.667=−0.667, bias2=0.444^2 = 0.4442=0.444 (it is the convexity of fff that causes it, the neighbors on both sides lie above the value at the center), variance 0.25/3=0.08330.25/3 = 0.08330.25/3=0.0833; total 0.25+0.444+0.083=0.7780.25 + 0.444 + 0.083 = 0.7780.25+0.444+0.083=0.778. For k=5k = 5k=5: all points, average (0+1+4+9+16)/5=6(0 + 1 + 4 + 9 + 16)/5 = 6(0+1+4+9+16)/5=6, bias2=4^2 = 42=4, variance 0.05, total 4.30. The best kkk at this point is the smallest: the noise is small relative to the curvature of fff.

With Python. The check below also simulates the whole process: it generates 100,000 training sets (new noise each time), predicts at x0=2x_0 = 2x0​=2 and measures the squared error against a fresh noisy target.

x_design = np.arange(5.0)
f_true = lambda x: x ** 2
sigma2, x0 = 0.25, 2.0
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
reps = 100_000
noise = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(sigma2), size=(reps, 5))
y_new = f_true(x0) + rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(sigma2), size=reps)
order = np.argsort(np.abs(x_design - x0), kind="stable")

rows = []
for k in (1, 3, 5):
    nn = order[:k]
    bias = f_true(x0) - f_true(x_design[nn]).mean()
    pred = (f_true(x_design)[None, :] + noise)[:, nn].mean(axis=1)
    rows.append({"k": k, "bias^2 (formula)": bias ** 2, "variance (formula)": sigma2 / k,
                 "total (formula)": sigma2 + bias ** 2 + sigma2 / k, "simulated mean squared error": np.mean((y_new - pred) ** 2)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4).to_string(index=False))
 k  bias^2 (formula)  variance (formula)  total (formula)  simulated mean squared error
 1            0.0000              0.2500           0.5000                        0.5002
 3            0.4444              0.0833           0.7778                        0.7808
 5            4.0000              0.0500           4.3000                        4.3082

The simulation agrees with the formula to within about 0.2%.

4.5.3 Checking the formulas on a whole function¶

Now we let x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​ vary. We use the simulated world f(x)=sin⁡(2πx)f(x) = \sin(2\pi x)f(x)=sin(2πx) on [0,1][0, 1][0,1], noise σ=0.3\sigma = 0.3σ=0.3 (so σ2=0.09\sigma^2 = 0.09σ2=0.09), and n=100n = 100n=100 equally spaced training inputs xi=(i−12)/nx_i = (i - \tfrac12)/nxi​=(i−21​)/n. Because the formula of Section 4.5.2 is exact, we can compute the bias and the variance at every x0x_0x0​ in closed form, average them over x0∈[0,1]x_0 \in [0, 1]x0​∈[0,1], and then confirm them by brute force, generating thousands of training sets. Figure 4.5 shows the fits obtained from 30 different training sets for three values of kkk.

def f_sin(x):
    return np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)


N_DESIGN, SIGMA = 100, 0.3
x_design = (np.arange(N_DESIGN) + 0.5) / N_DESIGN                   # fixed design: equally spaced inputs
x_grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 401)                                      # the points x0 where we evaluate the fit


def neighbor_indices(x_train, x_query, k):
    """Indices of the k nearest training inputs of each query point (1-D inputs, ties broken by position)."""
    dist = np.abs(x_train[None, :] - x_query[:, None])
    return np.argsort(dist, axis=1, kind="stable")[:, :k]


def exact_decomposition(k, n=N_DESIGN, sigma=SIGMA, x_query=x_grid):
    """Average over x0 of the bias^2 and of the variance of k-NN regression with a fixed design (formulas of Section 4.5.2)."""
    x_train = (np.arange(n) + 0.5) / n
    nn = neighbor_indices(x_train, x_query, k)
    bias2 = (f_sin(x_query) - f_sin(x_train)[nn].mean(axis=1)) ** 2
    return bias2.mean(), sigma ** 2 / k


rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
n_sets = 3000
y_sets = f_sin(x_design)[None, :] + rng.normal(0, SIGMA, size=(n_sets, N_DESIGN))      # 3000 training sets (only the targets change)
fits = {k: y_sets[:, neighbor_indices(x_design, x_grid, k)].mean(axis=2) for k in (1, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20, 30, 50)}   # (3000, 401) fits for each k

rows = []
for k, pred in fits.items():
    b2_exact, var_exact = exact_decomposition(k)
    y_fresh = f_sin(x_grid)[None, :] + rng.normal(0, SIGMA, size=pred.shape)
    rows.append({"k": k, "bias^2 exact": b2_exact, "bias^2 simulated": np.mean((pred.mean(axis=0) - f_sin(x_grid)) ** 2),
                 "variance exact": var_exact, "variance simulated": pred.var(axis=0).mean(),
                 "test MSE exact": SIGMA ** 2 + b2_exact + var_exact, "test MSE simulated": np.mean((y_fresh - pred) ** 2)})
check = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(check.round(4).to_string(index=False))
 k  bias^2 exact  bias^2 simulated  variance exact  variance simulated  test MSE exact  test MSE simulated

 8        0.0019            0.0020          0.0112              0.0113          0.1032              0.1030

# Figure 4.5 — thirty fits of k-NN regression, from thirty different training sets
def figure_4_5():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12.4, 3.9), sharey=True)
    for ax, k in zip(axes, [1, 12, 50]):
        for r in range(30):
            ax.plot(x_grid, fits[k][r], color=SKY, alpha=0.45, linewidth=0.9, label="30 individual fits" if r == 0 else None)
        ax.plot(x_grid, fits[k].mean(axis=0), color=VERMILION, linewidth=2.2, linestyle="--", label="average fit (3000 sets)")
        ax.plot(x_grid, f_sin(x_grid), color="black", linewidth=2, label="true $f$")
        b2, var = exact_decomposition(k)
        ax.set_title(f"k = {k}:  bias$^2$ = {b2:.3f},  variance = {var:.3f}", fontsize=10.5)
        ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("prediction")
    axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8.5, loc="lower left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_4_5()

In the left panel (k=1k = 1k=1) every fit is a noisy staircase: the thirty curves scatter widely around the truth, but their average (dashed) lies on top of it. The bias is nearly zero and the variance is large: 0.090=σ20.090 = \sigma^20.090=σ2, as predicted. In the right panel (k=50k = 50k=50) the fits are almost identical to one another (variance 0.002) but all of them are wrong in the same way, flattening the peaks of the sine: the bias is large and the variance small. The middle panel (k=12k = 12k=12) is a good compromise. Note also, at the ends of the interval, where all neighbors lie on one side of x0x_0x0​, the average fit sits below the peak of the curve even for k=12k = 12k=12: this is the boundary effect that we saw in Figure 4.4.

The table printed before the figure compares, for eight values of kkk, the exact formulas with a brute-force simulation of 3,000 training sets. The agreement is to three or four decimals for every entry: the decomposition is not a heuristic but an identity.

Because the formulas are exact, we can compute the whole curve for every kkk from 1 to 100 and find the best one, without any simulation. Figure 4.6 is the central picture of this chapter.

ks_all = np.arange(1, 101)
decomp = pd.DataFrame([(k, *exact_decomposition(k)) for k in ks_all], columns=["k", "bias2", "variance"]).set_index("k")
decomp["expected test MSE"] = SIGMA ** 2 + decomp["bias2"] + decomp["variance"]
k_best = int(decomp["expected test MSE"].idxmin())
print(f"noise sigma^2 = {SIGMA ** 2:.4f}")
print(f"best k = {k_best}: bias^2 = {decomp.loc[k_best, 'bias2']:.4f}, variance = {decomp.loc[k_best, 'variance']:.4f}, "
      f"expected test MSE = {decomp.loc[k_best, 'expected test MSE']:.4f}")
print(f"k = 1 : expected test MSE = {decomp.loc[1, 'expected test MSE']:.4f}  (twice the noise level: {2 * SIGMA ** 2:.4f})")
print(f"k = 100: expected test MSE = {decomp.loc[100, 'expected test MSE']:.4f}  (it predicts the mean of f, which is 0)")
print("k where the bias^2 equals the variance:", int((decomp['bias2'] - decomp['variance']).abs().idxmin()))

figure_4_6()

Reading the figure. The variance (dash-dot) falls like 1/k1/k1/k and the bias2^22 (dashed) rises with kkk: it is negligible while the neighborhood is narrow compared with the wavelength of the sine, and grows fast once the neighborhood spans a good part of a period. Their sum plus the noise (black) is U-shaped, with a minimum at k=10k = 10k=10, where the expected test error is 0.1025, only 0.0125 above the noise floor σ2=0.09\sigma^2 = 0.09σ2=0.09. The two extremes are bad for opposite reasons: k=1k = 1k=1 costs twice the noise, because the variance equals σ2\sigma^2σ2, and k=100k = 100k=100 (the global mean) gives an expected error of 0.59, almost six times that of the best kkk, because the bias is almost the whole variance of the signal. This U-shape is the model-complexity curve that has appeared in every chapter so far (Figures 1.4 and 3.3), now with an exact formula behind it. A very useful rule of thumb is visible: at the best kkk the bias2^22 (0.0035) and the variance (0.0090) are of the same order (they are equal at k=13k = 13k=13, a little to the right of the minimum, because the bias grows faster than the variance falls); a method whose variance is far larger than its squared bias is too flexible, and the opposite means it is too rigid.

4.5.4 The best kkk grows with nnn, while the neighborhoods shrink¶

How does the best kkk change when we have more data? Take the same sine and the same σ\sigmaσ, with n=25,50,…,12,800n = 25, 50, \dots, 12{,}800n=25,50,…,12,800 equally spaced inputs, compute the exact curves, and find for each nnn the kkk that minimizes the expected error and the error it achieves (we report the excess error over the noise floor, bias2+σ2/k\text{bias}^2 + \sigma^2/kbias2+σ2/k, which is what the method is responsible for).

def excess_curve(n, x_query):
    """Exact excess risk bias^2 + sigma^2/k of fixed-design k-NN regression, for every k = 1..n, averaged over x_query."""
    x_train = (np.arange(n) + 0.5) / n
    order = np.argsort(np.abs(x_train[None, :] - x_query[:, None]), axis=1, kind="stable")
    k = np.arange(1, n + 1)
    mean_of_f = np.cumsum(f_sin(x_train)[order], axis=1) / k[None, :]          # average of f over the k nearest, for every k at once
    return ((f_sin(x_query)[:, None] - mean_of_f) ** 2).mean(axis=0) + SIGMA ** 2 / k


ns = np.array([25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200, 6400, 12800])
region_grids = {"whole interval [0, 1]": np.linspace(0, 1, 401), "interior [0.2, 0.8]": np.linspace(0.2, 0.8, 241)}
best = {}
for name, grid in region_grids.items():
    ks_best, risks = [], []
    for n in ns:
        curve = excess_curve(n, grid)
        ks_best.append(int(curve.argmin()) + 1); risks.append(curve.min())
    best[name] = (np.array(ks_best), np.array(risks))
    slope_k = np.polyfit(np.log(ns), np.log(ks_best), 1)[0]
    slope_r = np.polyfit(np.log(ns), np.log(risks), 1)[0]
    print(f"{name}: slope of log k* against log n = {slope_k:.2f} | slope of log(excess error) against log n = {slope_r:.2f}")

summary = pd.DataFrame({"n": ns, "best k (whole interval)": best["whole interval [0, 1]"][0], "k/n": best["whole interval [0, 1]"][0] / ns,
                        "excess error": best["whole interval [0, 1]"][1]})
print(summary.round(4).to_string(index=False))

def figure_4_7():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 4.4))
    styles = {"whole interval [0, 1]": (BLUE, "o", "-"), "interior [0.2, 0.8]": (VERMILION, "s", "--")}
    for ax, idx, ylabel in [(axes[0], 0, "best number of neighbors $k^\\ast$"), (axes[1], 1, "excess error of the best $k$")]:
        for name, (color, marker, ls) in styles.items():
            ax.plot(ns, best[name][idx], color=color, marker=marker, linestyle=ls, linewidth=2, label=name)
        for slope, color, label in [(4 / 5, "gray", "slope 4/5"), (2 / 3, "black", "slope 2/3")]:
            sign = 1 if idx == 0 else -1
            ref = best["interior [0.2, 0.8]"][idx][0] * (ns / ns[0]) ** (sign * slope)
            ax.plot(ns, ref * (1.6 if idx == 0 else 1.6), color=color, linestyle=":", linewidth=1.4, label=f"reference, {label}" if idx == 0 else None)
        ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
        ax.set(xlabel="sample size $n$", ylabel=ylabel)
    axes[0].set_title("(a) the best $k$ grows with $n$")
    axes[1].set_title("(b) the best error falls with $n$")
    axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9.5)

figure_4_7()

More data call for a larger kkk, but a smaller neighborhood. The best number of neighbors grows with nnn (Figure 4.7a: from 4 at n=25n = 25n=25 to 356 at n=12,800n = 12{,}800n=12,800), and so does the number of points averaged, which kills the variance; yet the fraction k/nk/nk/n of the data that is used falls, from 0.16 to 0.03 (see the table), and with it the width of the neighborhood, which kills the bias. With more data we can afford both: more points in smaller neighborhoods. In the language of Chapter 3: with more data the model can become more flexible (the neighborhood shrinks, the approximation error falls) and more stable (more points per average, the estimation error falls) at the same time.

The slopes in Figure 4.7 can be explained with a short heuristic argument. Suppose that the function fff is smooth and that kkk neighbors occupy an interval of half-width h≈k/(2n)h \approx k/(2n)h≈k/(2n) around x0x_0x0​ (for equally spaced inputs). In the interior the neighbors lie on both sides, the first-order differences f(xi)−f(x0)f(x_i) - f(x_0)f(xi​)−f(x0​) cancel, and the bias is of the order of f′′ h2∝(k/n)2f''\,h^2 \propto (k/n)^2f′′h2∝(k/n)2, so that

bias2+variance  ≈  c(kn)4+σ2k.\text{bias}^2 + \text{variance} \;\approx\; c\Big(\frac{k}{n}\Big)^{4} + \frac{\sigma^2}{k}.bias2+variance≈c(nk​)4+kσ2​.
(6)

Setting the derivative with respect to kkk to zero gives k∗∝n4/5k^\ast \propto n^{4/5}k∗∝n4/5 and an excess error ∝n−4/5\propto n^{-4/5}∝n−4/5. Near the boundary the neighbors lie on one side, the first-order terms do not cancel, the bias is of order f′ h∝k/nf'\,h \propto k/nf′h∝k/n, and the same argument gives k∗∝n2/3k^\ast \propto n^{2/3}k∗∝n2/3 and an error ∝n−2/3\propto n^{-2/3}∝n−2/3. The measured slopes lie where we should expect them: about 0.79 in the interior, close to 4/54/54/5, and 0.73 over the whole interval, between 2/32/32/3 and 4/54/54/5, because the average over the interval includes a boundary region whose weight shrinks only slowly. (The slopes of the error, dotted lines in panel (b), are -0.81 and -0.74.) For comparison, a parametric model whose form is correct (a line, for data that are linear) has an excess error ∝1/n\propto 1/n∝1/n: the price of not knowing the form of the function is an error that decreases more slowly, as n−4/5n^{-4/5}n−4/5 at best. We will see in Section 4.7 how the exponent deteriorates with the dimension.

4.6 Consistency and the Bayes risk¶

Is the k-NN rule good, in the sense of Chapter 3: does its error approach the best possible one, R∗R^\astR∗, as the data grow? The answer has two parts, and it is a classical result.

4.6.1 The nearest-neighbor rule is at most twice as bad as Bayes¶

Let the labels be binary, y∈{0,1}y \in \{0, 1\}y∈{0,1}, let η(x)=P(y=1∣x)\eta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{P}(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})η(x)=P(y=1∣x) as in Section 3.2, and write r(x)=min⁡{η(x),1−η(x)}r(\mathbf{x}) = \min\{\eta(\mathbf{x}), 1 - \eta(\mathbf{x})\}r(x)=min{η(x),1−η(x)}, so that the Bayes risk is R∗=E[r(x)]R^\ast = \mathbb{E}[r(\mathbf{x})]R∗=E[r(x)].

Theorem 4.1 (Cover and Hart, 1967). As n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞ the risk of the 1-nearest-neighbor rule converges to

R1-NN=E[ 2 η(x) (1−η(x)) ],andR∗  ≤  R1-NN  ≤  2R∗(1−R∗)  ≤  2R∗.R_{1\text{-NN}} = \mathbb{E}\big[\,2\,\eta(\mathbf{x})\,(1 - \eta(\mathbf{x}))\,\big], \qquad\text{and}\qquad R^\ast \;\le\; R_{1\text{-NN}} \;\le\; 2R^\ast(1 - R^\ast) \;\le\; 2R^\ast .R1-NN​=E[2η(x)(1−η(x))],andR∗≤R1-NN​≤2R∗(1−R∗)≤2R∗.
(7)
Proof (sketch)

The limit. For a fixed test point x\mathbf{x}x, as nnn grows the nearest training point x(1)\mathbf{x}_{(1)}x(1)​ gets arbitrarily close to x\mathbf{x}x (this holds with probability one for every x\mathbf{x}x in the support of the distribution of the inputs), so that η(x(1))→η(x)\eta(\mathbf{x}_{(1)}) \to \eta(\mathbf{x})η(x(1)​)→η(x) if η\etaη is continuous. The label of the neighbor, y(1)y_{(1)}y(1)​, and the label yyy of the test point are then independent draws from the same Bernoulli distribution with parameter η(x)\eta(\mathbf{x})η(x) (given the inputs, the labels are independent). The rule errs when they differ, which has probability η(1−η)+(1−η)η=2η(1−η)\eta(1 - \eta) + (1 - \eta)\eta = 2\eta(1 - \eta)η(1−η)+(1−η)η=2η(1−η). Averaging over x\mathbf{x}x gives the formula. (A complete proof needs only that the nearest-neighbor distance tends to zero in probability, and handles discontinuous η\etaη with a measure-theoretic argument.)

The bounds. Since 2η(1−η)=2 r (1−r)2\eta(1-\eta) = 2\,r\,(1 - r)2η(1−η)=2r(1−r), R1-NN=2R∗−2 E[r2]R_{1\text{-NN}} = 2R^\ast - 2\,\mathbb{E}[r^2]R1-NN​=2R∗−2E[r2]. Jensen’s inequality gives E[r2]≥(E r)2=(R∗)2\mathbb{E}[r^2] \ge (\mathbb{E}\, r)^2 = (R^\ast)^2E[r2]≥(Er)2=(R∗)2, hence R1-NN≤2R∗−2(R∗)2=2R∗(1−R∗)R_{1\text{-NN}} \le 2R^\ast - 2(R^\ast)^2 = 2R^\ast(1 - R^\ast)R1-NN​≤2R∗−2(R∗)2=2R∗(1−R∗). For the lower bound note that 2r(1−r)≥r2r(1 - r) \ge r2r(1−r)≥r because r≤12r \le \tfrac12r≤21​. □\square□

This is remarkable: a method that never learns anything, with enough data, makes at most twice the error of the best possible classifier whatever the distribution. If the Bayes risk is 5%, the nearest-neighbor risk is at most 9.75%; if there is no noise at all (R∗=0R^\ast = 0R∗=0), the 1-NN rule is eventually perfect. The factor of 2 is the same fact as in Section 4.5.2: the variance of a single neighbor is as large as the noise.

4.6.2 Larger kkk closes the gap: Stone’s theorem¶

If we average more neighbors, the extra error disappears. For odd kkk the labels of the kkk neighbors are, in the limit, kkk independent Bernoulli(η\etaη) draws, and the rule errs when the majority disagrees with the label of the test point:

Rk-NN=E[η P(Bin(k,η)≤k−12)+(1−η) P(Bin(k,η)≥k+12)].R_{k\text{-NN}} = \mathbb{E}\Big[\eta\,\mathbb{P}\big(\mathrm{Bin}(k, \eta) \le \tfrac{k-1}{2}\big) + (1 - \eta)\,\mathbb{P}\big(\mathrm{Bin}(k, \eta) \ge \tfrac{k+1}{2}\big)\Big].Rk-NN​=E[ηP(Bin(k,η)≤2k−1​)+(1−η)P(Bin(k,η)≥2k+1​)].
(8)

This decreases with kkk and tends to R∗R^\astR∗. For kkk that grows with nnn the result is complete:

Theorem 4.2 (Stone, 1977). If k=kn→∞k = k_n \to \inftyk=kn​→∞ and kn/n→0k_n/n \to 0kn​/n→0, the k-NN rule is universally consistent: for every distribution of (x,y)(\mathbf{x}, y)(x,y), R(f^kn)→R∗R(\hat f_{k_n}) \to R^\astR(f^​kn​​)→R∗ as n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞ (and for regression, with the squared loss, R(f^kn)→R∗R(\hat f_{k_n}) \to R^\astR(f^​kn​​)→R∗ as well, if E[y2]<∞\mathbb{E}[y^2] < \inftyE[y2]<∞).

The two conditions are the two halves of the trade-off: k→∞k \to \inftyk→∞ makes the variance vanish, k/n→0k/n \to 0k/n→0 makes the neighborhoods shrink and the bias vanish. The proof is beyond this book (see the references), but the experiment below shows the theorem at work. It is a statement of a very different kind from the No Free Lunch theorem of Section 3.9: without any assumption on the distribution, the error tends to its best possible value. There is no contradiction: Theorem 3.8 averaged over all targets for a fixed sample size, while consistency is a statement about n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞, and it says nothing about how fast: for a general distribution the convergence can be arbitrarily slow (Devroye’s “no free lunch for rates”). The rates of Section 4.5.4 need assumptions on the smoothness of fff.

An experiment (simulated, because we need a world where R∗R^\astR∗ is known). The inputs are one-dimensional, the two classes are equally likely, and x∣y∼N(2y,1)x \mid y \sim \mathcal{N}(2y, 1)x∣y∼N(2y,1): this is the setting of Worked example 3.1 with the means 0 and 2, for which the Bayes risk is Φ(−1)=0.1587\Phi(-1) = 0.1587Φ(−1)=0.1587. We compute by numerical integration the three limits of the theory, R∗R^\astR∗, R1-NNR_{1\text{-NN}}R1-NN​ and R3-NNR_{3\text{-NN}}R3-NN​, and the bound 2R∗(1−R∗)2R^\ast(1 - R^\ast)2R∗(1−R∗), and then train k-NN with k=1k = 1k=1, k=3k = 3k=3, k≈nk \approx \sqrt{n}k≈n​ and k≈n2/3k \approx n^{2/3}k≈n2/3 on training sets of growing size, measuring the error on 20,000 fresh points.

from scipy.stats import binom

MU = 2.0                                                       # x | y ~ N(MU*y, 1), equal priors


def eta_world(x):
    p1, p0 = stats.norm.pdf(x, MU, 1), stats.norm.pdf(x, 0, 1)
    return p1 / (p0 + p1)


xs = np.linspace(-10, 12, 400_001)
dx = xs[1] - xs[0]
density = 0.5 * (stats.norm.pdf(xs, 0, 1) + stats.norm.pdf(xs, MU, 1))
eta_x = eta_world(xs)


def limit_risk(k):
    """Limiting risk of the k-NN rule (k odd) in this world, by numerical integration of the formula above."""
    p_majority_1 = 1 - binom.cdf((k - 1) // 2, k, eta_x)
    return np.sum(density * (eta_x * (1 - p_majority_1) + (1 - eta_x) * p_majority_1)) * dx


R_bayes = np.sum(density * np.minimum(eta_x, 1 - eta_x)) * dx
limits = {"Bayes risk $R^*$": R_bayes, "3-NN limit": limit_risk(3), "1-NN limit": limit_risk(1), "Cover-Hart bound $2R^*(1-R^*)$": 2 * R_bayes * (1 - R_bayes)}
for name, value in limits.items():
    print(f"{name:<34}{value:.4f}")
print("check: Phi(-MU/2) =", round(stats.norm.cdf(-MU / 2), 4), "| 5-NN limit:", round(limit_risk(5), 4), "| 25-NN limit:", round(limit_risk(25), 4))

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)


def draw_world(n):
    y = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
    return (rng.normal(0, 1, n) + MU * y)[:, None], y


X_fresh, y_fresh = draw_world(20_000)
sizes = [10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000]
rule = {"k = 1": lambda n: 1, "k = 3": lambda n: 3,
        "k ≈ √n": lambda n: min(int(round(np.sqrt(n))) | 1, n), "k ≈ n^(2/3)": lambda n: min(int(round(n ** (2 / 3))) | 1, n)}
rows = []
for n in sizes:
    errors = {name: [] for name in rule}
    for _ in range(20 if n <= 1000 else 6):
        X_s, y_s = draw_world(n)
        for name, k_of_n in rule.items():
            errors[name].append(np.mean(KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k_of_n(n)).fit(X_s, y_s).predict(X_fresh) != y_fresh))
    rows.append({"n": n, **{name: np.mean(v) for name, v in errors.items()}})
consistency = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(consistency.round(4).to_string(index=False))

1-NN limit                        0.2248

check: Phi(-MU/2) = 0.1587 | 5-NN limit: 0.1802 | 25-NN limit: 0.1634

def figure_4_8():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.8))
    styles = {"k = 1": (VERMILION, "o", "-"), "k = 3": (ORANGE, "^", "-"), "k ≈ √n": (BLUE, "s", "--"), "k ≈ n^(2/3)": (GREEN, "D", "-.")}
    for name, (color, marker, ls) in styles.items():

figure_4_8()

Reading the figure. Three facts stand out. (1) The curves of the two fixed values of kkk stop improving after n≈100n \approx 100n≈100 and settle at their theoretical limits: about 0.222 for k=1k = 1k=1 (the limit is 0.225) and 0.189 for k=3k = 3k=3 (the limit is 0.192). Having more data does not help a method whose kkk is stuck: its error is limited by the variance of a few neighbors, not by the amount of data. Both limits are above the Bayes risk of 0.159 and below the Cover–Hart bound of 0.267, as Theorem 4.1 says. (2) The two curves with a growing kkk approach the Bayes risk: at n=10,000n = 10{,}000n=10,000 they are at 0.157 (k≈n=101k \approx \sqrt{n} = 101k≈n​=101) and 0.157 (k≈n2/3=465k \approx n^{2/3} = 465k≈n2/3=465), indistinguishable from 0.159 within the sampling error of the experiment (about 0.003, because the test set has 20,000 points; that is also why a value slightly below R∗R^\astR∗ is possible). (3) At very small nnn a large kkk can hurt: for n=10n = 10n=10 the rule k≈n2/3k \approx n^{2/3}k≈n2/3 takes k=5k = 5k=5 neighbors out of 10 points and is worse than k=3k = 3k=3. Consistency is a statement about n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞; for each finite nnn the best kkk must still be found from the data, which is what Chapter 5 is about.

4.7 The curse of dimensionality¶

Everything so far worked with one or two features, or with Digits, where 64 features turned out to be harmless. The main weakness of local methods appears when the number of features ddd grows: “close” stops being a useful notion. The phenomenon is called the curse of dimensionality (Bellman, 1961), and it has three faces.

4.7.1 Three faces of the curse¶

1. Neighborhoods are not local. Suppose the inputs are uniform in the unit cube [0,1]d[0, 1]^d[0,1]d, and we want a neighborhood (a sub-cube) that contains a fraction ppp of the data. Its side must be p1/dp^{1/d}p1/d. For p=1%p = 1\%p=1% the side is 0.01 in dimension 1, 0.10 in dimension 2, 0.63 in dimension 10 and 0.95 in dimension 100: to capture 1% of the data in 100 dimensions we need a cube that spans 95% of the range of every feature. That is not a neighborhood any more. To have kkk neighbors in a neighborhood of a given absolute side sss we need n≈k/sdn \approx k/s^dn≈k/sd data points: the sample size grows exponentially with ddd.

2. Distances concentrate. In high dimensions the distance from a point to its nearest neighbor becomes almost as large as the distance to a typical point. If all points are about equally far, the notion of “nearest” loses its meaning (Beyer et al., 1999). The next cell measures it: it draws n=1,000n = 1{,}000n=1,000 points uniformly in [0,1]d[0, 1]^d[0,1]d (a simulation), and compares, for 200 query points, the distance to the nearest point with the average distance to all the points.

3. Slow rates. The heuristic argument of Section 4.5.4 for a smooth function in ddd dimensions says that the kkk neighbors lie within a radius r∝(k/n)1/dr \propto (k/n)^{1/d}r∝(k/n)1/d, the bias is of order r2=(k/n)2/dr^2 = (k/n)^{2/d}r2=(k/n)2/d, so that bias2+variance≈c (k/n)4/d+σ2/k\text{bias}^2 + \text{variance} \approx c\,(k/n)^{4/d} + \sigma^2/kbias2+variance≈c(k/n)4/d+σ2/k. Minimizing over kkk gives k∗∝n4/(d+4)k^\ast \propto n^{4/(d+4)}k∗∝n4/(d+4) and an excess error ∝n−4/(d+4)\propto n^{-4/(d+4)}∝n−4/(d+4): for d=1d = 1d=1 the exponent is 4/54/54/5 of Section 4.5.4, for d=10d = 10d=10 it is 4/14≈0.294/14 \approx 0.294/14≈0.29. (For merely Lipschitz functions the exponent is 2/(d+2)2/(d + 2)2/(d+2), and this is the best possible rate for any method over that class of functions: it is not a weakness of k-NN but of local learning with no other assumption.) Ignoring constants, the number of examples needed to reach the error obtained with n0n_0n0​ examples in dimension 1 is n0(d+4)/5n_0^{(d+4)/5}n0(d+4)/5​.

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
rows = []
for d in [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500, 1000]:
    X_u, Q_u = rng.random((1000, d)), rng.random((200, d))
    D = np.sqrt(np.maximum((Q_u ** 2).sum(1)[:, None] + (X_u ** 2).sum(1)[None, :] - 2 * Q_u @ X_u.T, 0))   # (200, 1000) distances
    rows.append({"d": d, "nearest": D.min(axis=1).mean(), "average": D.mean(axis=1).mean(), "nearest / average": (D.min(axis=1) / D.mean(axis=1)).mean(),
                 "side for 1% of the data": 0.01 ** (1 / d), "side for 10% of the data": 0.1 ** (1 / d)})
concentration = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("d")
print(concentration.round(3).to_string())

n0 = 100
need = pd.DataFrame({"exponent 4/(d+4)": [4 / (d + 4) for d in (1, 2, 5, 10, 20)],
                     f"n needed to match n = {n0} at d = 1": [f"{n0 ** ((d + 4) / 5):,.0f}" for d in (1, 2, 5, 10, 20)]}, index=pd.Index([1, 2, 5, 10, 20], name="d"))
print()
print(need.round(2).to_string())

# Figure 4.9 — the geometry of high dimensions
def figure_4_9():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 4.3))
    d_axis = np.arange(1, 201)
    for p, color, ls in [(0.01, VERMILION, "-"), (0.1, BLUE, "--")]:
        axes[0].plot(d_axis, p ** (1 / d_axis), color=color, linestyle=ls, linewidth=2.2, label=f"to capture {p:.0%} of the data")
    axes[0].set(xlabel="dimension $d$", ylabel="side of the sub-cube (range of each feature = 1)", title="(a) a 'local' neighborhood is not local", ylim=(0, 1.02))
    axes[0].legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
    axes[1].plot(concentration.index, concentration["nearest / average"], color=GREEN, marker="o", linewidth=2)
    axes[1].set_xscale("log")
    axes[1].set(xlabel="dimension $d$ (log scale)", ylabel="distance to the nearest point / average distance",
                title="(b) the nearest point is as far as a typical one (simulated, n = 1000)", ylim=(0, 1.02))
    axes[1].title.set_fontsize(11)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_4_9()

Panel (a) is the first face: the side of the sub-cube that contains 1% of the data goes from 0.01 to practically the whole range as ddd grows, and the one for 10% of the data is already at 0.79 in dimension 10. Panel (b), a simulation, is the second face: the ratio between the distance to the nearest point and the average distance rises from 0.002 in dimension 1 (the nearest of 1,000 points is almost on top of the query) to 0.40 in dimension 10, 0.73 in dimension 50 and 0.94 in dimension 1,000, where the nearest of the thousand points is only 6% closer than the average one. The last table is the third face, under the idealized assumptions of the heuristic (the constants are ignored): the exponent of the rate falls from 0.8 in dimension 1 to 0.29 in dimension 10, and the sample size that is needed to match the accuracy obtained with 100 examples in dimension 1 is about 250 in dimension 2, 4,000 in dimension 5, 400,000 in dimension 10 and 4 billion in dimension 20.

4.7.2 The curse on real data: irrelevant features¶

The curse is not only about the number of features, but about the number of useful ones. A distance counts every feature equally, so each irrelevant feature adds noise to the distance and moves the points apart without telling the classes apart. We measure it with a real data set, Breast Cancer (30 features, standardized inside the pipeline), to which we append mmm columns of pure noise (N(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1)N(0,1), independent of the label). We compare 5-NN with logistic regression (a linear model, Chapter 6), which is not based on distances, on 15 random stratified splits.

from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X_bc, y_bc = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
rows = []
for m_noise in [0, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000]:
    acc_knn, acc_lin = [], []
    for r in range(15):
        noise_cols = np.random.default_rng(r).normal(size=(len(X_bc), m_noise))
        Z = np.hstack([X_bc, noise_cols]) if m_noise else X_bc
        Za, Zb, ya, yb = train_test_split(Z, y_bc, test_size=0.3, random_state=r, stratify=y_bc)
        acc_knn.append(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)).fit(Za, ya).score(Zb, yb))
        acc_lin.append(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000)).fit(Za, ya).score(Zb, yb))
    rows.append({"noise features": m_noise, "5-NN": np.mean(acc_knn), "logistic regression": np.mean(acc_lin)})
noise_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(noise_table.round(4).to_string(index=False))
 noise features   5-NN  logistic regression
              0 0.9634               0.9727
             10 0.9505               0.9665
             30 0.9442               0.9622
            100 0.9103               0.9450
            300 0.8823               0.9396
           1000 0.8031               0.9232

The accuracy of 5-NN falls steadily as noise columns are added (from 0.963 to 0.803 with 1,000 of them), while logistic regression loses much less (from 0.973 to 0.923): a model that can learn a weight for each feature can, in principle, give a weight close to zero to a useless one, whereas a distance cannot. Even logistic regression suffers (it has more parameters to estimate from the same 398 training patients, Chapter 3), but k-NN suffers about three times as much. The lesson is practical: before using a distance-based method, remove the features that you know to be irrelevant, and consider automatic feature selection (Chapter 10) or a metric learned from the data.

4.7.3 Why Digits works: intrinsic dimension¶

Digits has 64 features, and yet 1-NN reaches 98.5%. Why does the curse not strike? Because the data do not fill the 64-dimensional space: images of digits are strongly constrained (neighboring pixels are correlated, and a handwritten digit has only a handful of “degrees of freedom”: slant, thickness, the shape of the loops...), so they lie close to a low-dimensional surface inside the space of pixels. What matters for k-NN is this intrinsic dimension, not the number of columns. We can check it by projecting the data on their first mmm principal components (Chapter 13 explains how they are obtained; here we only use them as a way of reducing the dimension) and measuring the accuracy of 5-NN on the projection, with the projection fitted on the training set only.

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

components = [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 64]
acc_pca = np.zeros((15, len(components)))
for r in range(15):
    Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(X_dg, y_dg, test_size=0.3, random_state=r, stratify=y_dg)
    for j, m_comp in enumerate(components):
        model = make_pipeline(PCA(n_components=m_comp, random_state=SEED), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)).fit(Xa, ya)
        acc_pca[r, j] = model.score(Xb, yb)
explained = np.cumsum(PCA().fit(X_dg).explained_variance_ratio_)
pca_table = pd.DataFrame({"components m": components, "5-NN accuracy": acc_pca.mean(axis=0),
                          "variance explained": [explained[m_ - 1] for m_ in components]})
print(pca_table.round(4).to_string(index=False))
 components m  5-NN accuracy  variance explained
            1         0.3341              0.1489
            2         0.6185              0.2851
            3         0.7572              0.4030
            5         0.9181              0.5450
            8         0.9586              0.6739
           10         0.9746              0.7382
           15         0.9802              0.8353
           20         0.9823              0.8943
           30         0.9826              0.9591
           40         0.9833              0.9882
