# Figure 4.10 — irrelevant features hurt k-NN; digits live in a low-dimensional subspace
def figure_4_10():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 4.3))
    ax = axes[0]
    ax.plot(noise_table["noise features"] + 30, noise_table["5-NN"], color=VERMILION, marker="o", linewidth=2, label="5-NN")
    ax.plot(noise_table["noise features"] + 30, noise_table["logistic regression"], color=BLUE, marker="s", linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="logistic regression")
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set(xlabel="total number of features (30 real + noise columns, log scale)", ylabel="test accuracy", title="(a) Breast Cancer plus noise features")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower left")
    ax = axes[1]
    ax.plot(pca_table["components m"], pca_table["5-NN accuracy"], color=GREEN, marker="o", linewidth=2)
    ax.axhline(acc_pca[:, -1].mean(), color="gray", linestyle=":", linewidth=1.4)
    ax.text(62, acc_pca[:, -1].mean() - 0.045, "all 64 pixels", ha="right", fontsize=9.5, color="dimgray")
    ax.set(xlabel="number of principal components $m$", ylabel="test accuracy of 5-NN", title="(b) Digits: a few components suffice")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_4_10()

Panel (a) shows the effect: with 1,000 noise columns, 97% of the features are useless, and 5-NN falls by 16 points while logistic regression falls by 5. Panel (b) shows why Digits is easy for k-NN: the accuracy of 5-NN on the projection on the first 10 principal components is already 0.975 (they capture 74% of the variance), with 20 components it reaches 0.982, as good as with all 64 pixels (0.983), and with a single component it is 0.33. The data behave as if they had an intrinsic dimension of the order of ten to twenty, which a method that relies on distances can exploit even though the number of columns is 64. The relevant dimension is the one that the data and the distance actually see, not the number of columns. This is why dimensionality reduction (Chapter 13) is often the first step before a nearest-neighbor method.

4.8 k-NN in practice¶

4.8.1 Choosing the distance and the weights¶

The Euclidean distance is the default, but nothing forces it. The Minkowski distance (∑j∣xj−xj′∣p)1/p\big(\sum_j \lvert x_j - x'_j\rvert^p\big)^{1/p}(∑j​∣xj​−xj′​∣p)1/p contains the Manhattan distance (p=1p = 1p=1), the Euclidean (p=2p = 2p=2) and, as p→∞p\to\inftyp→∞, the Chebyshev distance max⁡j∣xj−xj′∣\max_j \lvert x_j - x'_j\rvertmaxj​∣xj​−xj′​∣; the cosine distance 1−x⊤x′∥x∥ ∥x′∥1 - \frac{\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}'}{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{x}'\rVert}1−∥x∥∥x′∥x⊤x′​ compares directions and ignores magnitudes, which is natural for text or for images with variable brightness. The votes can also be weighted: with weights="distance" each neighbor counts 1/∥x−xi∥1/\lVert\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_i\rVert1/∥x−xi​∥, so that closer neighbors matter more (and a test point that coincides with a training point takes its label). A weighted k-NN is less sensitive to the exact value of kkk. We compare the options on Digits (raw pixels) and on Wine (all 13 features, standardized), with 20 random stratified splits each.

def compare_variants(X, y, variants, scale=False, n_repeats=20):
    """Mean and standard deviation of the test accuracy, over random stratified 70/30 splits, for each k-NN variant."""
    out = {}
    for name, kwargs in variants.items():
        accs = []
        for r in range(n_repeats):
            Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=r, stratify=y)
            model = KNeighborsClassifier(**kwargs)
            if scale:
                model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), model)
            accs.append(model.fit(Xa, ya).score(Xb, yb))
        out[name] = (np.mean(accs), np.std(accs))
    return out


variants = {"Euclidean, uniform votes": dict(n_neighbors=5),
            "Manhattan (p = 1)": dict(n_neighbors=5, p=1),
            "Minkowski p = 3": dict(n_neighbors=5, p=3),
            "Chebyshev (p = infinity)": dict(n_neighbors=5, metric="chebyshev"),
            "cosine": dict(n_neighbors=5, metric="cosine", algorithm="brute"),
            "Euclidean, distance-weighted votes": dict(n_neighbors=5, weights="distance")}
res_digits = compare_variants(X_dg, y_dg, variants)
res_wine = compare_variants(wine.data.to_numpy(), y_w, variants, scale=True)
variant_table = pd.DataFrame({"Digits (mean)": {k: v[0] for k, v in res_digits.items()}, "Digits (std)": {k: v[1] for k, v in res_digits.items()},
                              "Wine (mean)": {k: v[0] for k, v in res_wine.items()}, "Wine (std)": {k: v[1] for k, v in res_wine.items()}})
print(variant_table.round(4).to_string())
                                    Digits (mean)  Digits (std)  Wine (mean)  Wine (std)
Euclidean, uniform votes                   0.9833        0.0040       0.9602      0.0197
Manhattan (p = 1)                          0.9791        0.0045       0.9657      0.0134
Minkowski p = 3                            0.9829        0.0053       0.9509      0.0197
Chebyshev (p = infinity)                   0.9715        0.0076       0.9250      0.0290
cosine                                     0.9816        0.0050       0.9565      0.0213
Euclidean, distance-weighted votes         0.9836        0.0039       0.9630      0.0194

On Digits the Euclidean distance, the cosine distance, the Minkowski distance with p=3p = 3p=3 and the distance-weighted vote all give about 0.982 to 0.984, differences that are well inside the standard deviation over splits (0.004 to 0.005); the Manhattan distance is a little lower (0.979) and the Chebyshev distance is clearly the worst (0.972). On Wine the Manhattan distance is the best (0.966, against 0.960 for the Euclidean one), the weighted vote and the cosine distance are close to the Euclidean one, and again the Chebyshev distance is clearly worse (0.925, with a larger variability). The Chebyshev distance looks only at the single feature in which two points differ most, throwing away the information in the others, which is rarely what we want. The practical conclusion is not that one distance is best, but that the choice among reasonable distances matters much less than the choices of Section 4.7 (which features to include, and how to scale them), and that differences of a few tenths of a point between variants are not evidence of anything unless they are checked with a procedure designed for that (Chapter 5).

4.8.2 Scaling, and the choice of kkk¶

Two rules from earlier chapters apply in full. Scale the features (Section 2.7: on the Wine data one feature accounted for 99.8% of the squared distance before standardization), with the scaler fitted on the training set only, inside a pipeline. And choose kkk with held-out data, never with the training set (Figure 4.3: the training accuracy always picks k=1k = 1k=1); Chapter 5 shows how, with validation sets and cross-validation. As a starting point, for nnn examples, k≈nk \approx \sqrt{n}k≈n​ is a common rule of thumb (it satisfies the two conditions of Stone’s theorem), and for two classes an odd kkk avoids ties.

4.8.3 Speed: brute force against trees¶

A naive prediction costs O(nd)O(nd)O(nd) per query: for nnn in the millions this is too slow if many queries arrive. KD-trees (Bentley, 1975) and ball trees organize the training points in a hierarchy of boxes or balls, so that large parts of the data can be discarded without computing a distance, and the search takes about O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) in low dimensions. Their efficiency, however, is another face of the curse: as ddd grows the pruning stops working (all boxes look equally close, Section 4.7.1), and in high dimensions the tree is no better than brute force, and often worse. We measure it on n=20,000n = 20{,}000n=20,000 standard-Gaussian points and 500 queries, for k=5k = 5k=5, with the three algorithms of scikit-learn (the best of three repetitions; the times are in milliseconds and depend on your machine).

import time

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
rows = []
for d in [2, 5, 10, 20, 50]:
    X_t, Q_t = rng.normal(size=(20_000, d)), rng.normal(size=(500, d))
    row = {"d": d}
    for algorithm in ["brute", "kd_tree", "ball_tree"]:
        t_build, t_query = [], []
        for _ in range(3):
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            nn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5, algorithm=algorithm).fit(X_t, np.zeros(len(X_t), dtype=int))
            t1 = time.perf_counter()
            nn.kneighbors(Q_t)
            t_build.append(t1 - t0); t_query.append(time.perf_counter() - t1)
        row[f"{algorithm}: build"] = 1000 * min(t_build)
        row[f"{algorithm}: 500 queries"] = 1000 * min(t_query)
    rows.append(row)
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("d").round(1).to_string())
    brute: build  brute: 500 queries  kd_tree: build  kd_tree: 500 queries  ball_tree: build  ball_tree: 500 queries
d                                                                                                                   
2            0.5                 5.7             8.4                   1.3               7.3                     7.3
5            0.9                 5.5            10.0                   3.9               6.8                    22.4
10           0.6                 6.1            15.2                  36.3               9.7                    55.3
20           0.9                 6.3            27.2                 167.2              16.6                   110.9
50           1.3                 8.7            64.4                 344.5              35.8                   236.8

In the run printed above, the brute-force query time is almost independent of the dimension (10 to 19 ms for 500 queries: it is one matrix product and a partial sort), and there is no building cost. In dimension 2 the KD-tree answers the queries about ten times faster (1 ms), and the price of building it (5 ms) is repaid after a few hundred queries; in dimension 5 it is still faster than brute force by a factor of about 2.5; at d=10d = 10d=10 the trees are already slower than brute force, and from d=20d = 20d=20 on they are slower by one to two orders of magnitude. The numbers depend on the machine and on the library version, but the pattern is the general one: trees pay in low dimensions (roughly up to ten features) and not beyond, brute force is the right baseline otherwise, and scikit-learn’s default algorithm="auto" chooses among the three with simple rules based on the size and the dimension of the data.

Beyond a few tens of dimensions, exact search is replaced in practice by approximate nearest-neighbor methods (hashing, graph-based indexes), which give up the guarantee of returning exactly the nearest points in exchange for orders of magnitude of speed; they are the engine of similarity search in large collections of images, documents and embeddings.

4.9 Summary¶

  • The method. k-NN predicts at x\mathbf{x}x the average (regression) or the majority vote (classification) of the labels of the kkk training points closest to x\mathbf{x}x. It has no training phase; the training set is the model. A prediction costs O(nd)O(nd)O(nd) with brute force.

  • kkk is a smoothing parameter. k=1k = 1k=1 interpolates the training data (Voronoi cells, training error 0), large kkk flattens the fit toward the global mean or majority. The training error always selects k=1k = 1k=1 and cannot be used to choose kkk; the best kkk is found with held-out data (Chapter 5) and lies on a plateau that is wider and shifts to larger values when the data are noisier.

  • Bias–variance decomposition. For the squared loss, E[(y0−f^S(x0))2]=σ2+bias2+variance\mathbb{E}[(y_0 - \hat f_S(\mathbf{x}_0))^2] = \sigma^2 + \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance}E[(y0​−f^​S​(x0​))2]=σ2+bias2+variance: noise that no method can remove, systematic error of the average fit, sensitivity of the fit to the sample. Flexibility lowers the bias and raises the variance; the best model balances the two.

  • k-NN regression in closed form (fixed design): variance σ2/k\sigma^2/kσ2/k (so 1-NN doubles the unavoidable error) and bias equal to f(x0)f(\mathbf{x}_0)f(x0​) minus the average of fff over the neighbors. The best kkk grows with nnn (∝n4/5\propto n^{4/5}∝n4/5 in the interior for a smooth fff in one dimension, n2/3n^{2/3}n2/3 at the boundary), while k/nk/nk/n and the neighborhood width shrink.

  • Consistency. The 1-NN risk tends to E[2η(1−η)]≤2R∗(1−R∗)\mathbb{E}[2\eta(1-\eta)] \le 2R^\ast(1-R^\ast)E[2η(1−η)]≤2R∗(1−R∗) (Cover–Hart), and k-NN is universally consistent when k→∞k \to \inftyk→∞ and k/n→0k/n \to 0k/n→0 (Stone), with no assumption on the distribution; the rate depends on the smoothness of the problem and on the dimension.

  • The curse of dimensionality. In high dimensions neighborhoods are not local (a cube with 1% of the data spans 95% of each range at d=100d = 100d=100), distances concentrate (nearest ≈\approx≈ average), and the rate degrades to n−4/(d+4)n^{-4/(d+4)}n−4/(d+4) for smooth functions. What counts is the intrinsic dimension and the number of relevant features: noise features damage k-NN much more than a linear model (Breast Cancer: 0.963 to 0.803 against 0.973 to 0.923), and Digits works despite its 64 pixels because ten to twenty components carry the information.

  • In practice. Scale the features (fitted on the training set), remove irrelevant ones, choose kkk by validation, prefer brute force or a KD-tree according to ddd (trees pay up to about ten features), and treat the choice of the distance as a secondary matter. On Diabetes, least squares beat k-NN: a more flexible method wins only if the truth needs the flexibility, or if there is enough data to pay for it.

Data sources¶

  • Digits: E. Alpaydin and C. Kaynak, “Optical Recognition of Handwritten Digits”, UCI Machine Learning Repository (1998). The test portion of the data set, 1,797 images of 8×88\times88×8 pixels, is bundled with scikit-learn.

  • Wine: M. Forina et al., PARVUS: An Extendible Package for Data Exploration, Classification and Correlation, Institute of Pharmaceutical and Food Analysis and Technologies, Genoa (1991). Bundled with scikit-learn.

  • Diabetes: B. Efron, T. Hastie, I. Johnstone and R. Tibshirani, “Least Angle Regression”, Annals of Statistics (with discussion), 407–499 (2004). Bundled with scikit-learn; the ten features are centered and scaled by scikit-learn.

  • Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic): W. N. Street, W. H. Wolberg and O. L. Mangasarian, “Nuclear feature extraction for breast tumor diagnosis”, IS&T/SPIE 1993 International Symposium on Electronic Imaging: Science and Technology, volume 1905, 861–870 (1993). Bundled with scikit-learn. The 1,000 noise columns of Section 4.7.2 are added by us.

  • Simulated data: the sine world of Sections 4.5.3 and 4.5.4, the two-Gaussian world of Section 4.6.2, the uniform points of Section 4.7.1 and the points of the timing experiment of Section 4.8.3 are simulations, used because the theory needs a distribution or a function that is known exactly.

Further reading¶

  • E. Fix and J. L. Hodges, “Discriminatory analysis. Nonparametric discrimination: consistency properties”, Report 4, USAF School of Aviation Medicine, Randolph Field, Texas (1951). The origin of the nearest-neighbor rule.

  • T. M. Cover and P. E. Hart, “Nearest neighbor pattern classification”, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 13(1), 21–27 (1967). Theorem 4.1.

  • C. J. Stone, “Consistent nonparametric regression”, Annals of Statistics 5(4), 595–620 (1977). Theorem 4.2.

  • L. Devroye, L. Györfi and G. Lugosi, A Probabilistic Theory of Pattern Recognition, Springer, 1996. The reference on nearest-neighbor rules, with proofs of consistency and of the slow-rate results.

  • L. Györfi, M. Kohler, A. Krzyżak and H. Walk, A Distribution-Free Theory of Nonparametric Regression, Springer, 2002. Rates of convergence of k-NN and kernel regression.

  • T. Hastie, R. Tibshirani and J. Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Springer, 2009. Chapter 2 (local methods and the curse of dimensionality), Chapter 7 (bias–variance) and Chapter 13 (nearest-neighbor methods).

  • S. Geman, E. Bienenstock and R. Doursat, “Neural networks and the bias/variance dilemma”, Neural Computation 4(1), 1–58 (1992).

  • R. E. Bellman, Adaptive Control Processes: A Guided Tour, Princeton University Press, 1961. Where the “curse of dimensionality” was named.

  • K. Beyer, J. Goldstein, R. Ramakrishnan and U. Shaft, “When is ‘nearest neighbor’ meaningful?”, International Conference on Database Theory (ICDT), 217–235 (1999).

  • J. L. Bentley, “Multidimensional binary search trees used for associative searching”, Communications of the ACM 18(9), 509–517 (1975). The KD-tree.

  • K. Q. Weinberger and L. K. Saul, “Distance metric learning for large margin nearest neighbor classification”, Journal of Machine Learning Research 10, 207–244 (2009). Learning the metric from the data.

4.10 Exercises¶

Difficulty: ★ warm-up, ★★ core, ★★★ challenge. Try each exercise before reading the hint; solutions and detailed outlines are in Appendix C.

Manual (analytical) exercises¶

Exercise 4.1 ★ — k-NN by hand, with weights. One-dimensional training set: x=1,2,4,7,9,10x = 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 10x=1,2,4,7,9,10 with labels 0,0,1,1,0,00, 0, 1, 1, 0, 00,0,1,1,0,0. (a) Classify the query x=5x = 5x=5 with k=1,3,5k = 1, 3, 5k=1,3,5 and the Euclidean distance. (b) Classify it again with k=5k = 5k=5 and distance-weighted votes (each neighbor counts 1/∣x−xi∣1/\lvert x - x_i\rvert1/∣x−xi​∣). (c) What happens with k=6k = 6k=6 and uniform votes? Is the answer a property of the data or of the method? (d) What is the training error of 1-NN on this set? And of 6-NN?

Hint. List the six distances first and sort them; mind the tie at distance 4.

Exercise 4.2 ★ — Bias and variance at the boundary and in the interior. The training inputs are xi=(i−1)/100x_i = (i - 1)/100xi​=(i−1)/100, i=1,…,101i = 1, \dots, 101i=1,…,101 (so x∈[0,1]x \in [0, 1]x∈[0,1] with step 0.01), the true function is f(x)=xf(x) = xf(x)=x, and the noise has variance σ2=0.25\sigma^2 = 0.25σ2=0.25. (b) Do the same at the central point x0=0.5x_0 = 0.5x0​=0.5 for odd kkk. (c) Find the best kkk at each of the two points. What does the difference tell you about using a single kkk for the whole input range?

Hint. At x0=0x_0 = 0x0​=0 the kkk nearest neighbors are x1,…,xkx_1, \dots, x_kx1​,…,xk​, with average (k−1)/200(k - 1)/200(k−1)/200. At x0=0.5x_0 = 0.5x0​=0.5 the neighbors are symmetric and the average of the linear function equals f(x0)f(x_0)f(x0​).

A binary problem has η(x)=P(y=1∣x)\eta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{P}(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})η(x)=P(y=1∣x) equal to 0.9 on one half of the input space (in probability) and to 0.2 on the other half. Python (computational) exercises¶

Exercise 4.6 ★ — k-NN regression from scratch. Write knn_regress(X_train, y_train, X_test, k) that returns the average of the targets of the kkk nearest neighbors, using the Gram-matrix distances of Worked example 2.1 and np.argpartition. Compare it with KNeighborsRegressor on the 10 features of the Diabetes data, with 30 random 70/30 splits and k=20k = 20k=20: how often do the two sets of predictions coincide, and what is the mean test MSE?

Hint. Reuse the structure of knn_predict of Section 4.2.2; the prediction is y_train[nearest].mean(axis=1).

Exercise 4.7 ★★ — Bias and variance by simulation, with a random design. Let f(x)=I[x>0.5]f(x) = \mathbb{I}[x > 0.5]f(x)=I[x>0.5] (a step), σ=0.3\sigma = 0.3σ=0.3, and let the training inputs be random, xi∼U[0,1]x_i \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1]xi​∼U[0,1], n=100n = 100n=100. Generate 2,000 training sets. (a) For k-NN regression with k=1,5,10,20,50k = 1, 5, 10, 20, 50k=1,5,10,20,50 estimate, at x0=0.2x_0 = 0.2x0​=0.2 and at x0=0.5x_0 = 0.5x0​=0.5 (at the jump), the bias2^22, the variance and the expected test error. (b) Do the same for polynomial regression of degree 1,3,91, 3, 91,3,9 (np.polyfit). (c) Comment on where the bias comes from in each method and on which method is better at which point.

Hint. For each training set compute the prediction at the two points; the bias2^22 is (mean prediction −f(x0))2- f(x_0))^2−f(x0​))2, the variance is the variance of the prediction over the 2,000 sets, and the expected test error is σ2\sigma^2σ2 + bias2^22 + variance.

Exercise 4.8 ★★ — Kernel regression: fixed bandwidth against fixed kkk. The Nadaraya–Watson estimator replaces the “kkk nearest” by a smooth weighting with a bandwidth hhh: f^h(x)=∑iK((x−xi)/h) yi/∑iK((x−xi)/h)\hat f_h(x) = \sum_i K\big((x - x_i)/h\big)\,y_i\big/\sum_i K\big((x - x_i)/h\big)f^​h​(x)=∑i​K((x−xi​)/h)yi​/∑i​K((x−xi​)/h), with the Gaussian kernel K(u)=e−u2/2K(u) = e^{-u^2/2}K(u)=e−u2/2. (a) Implement it for the Diabetes data with the single feature bmi. (b) Find the best hhh on a grid with 20 random 70/30 splits and compare the test MSE with the best k-NN of Section 4.4 (about 3,966 for k=40k = 40k=40). (c) Plot the two fits on the whole data set. In which regions of the input do they differ most, and why? (Hint for (c): think about how many data points lie in a window of fixed width where the data are sparse.)

Hint. Guard against a division by zero far from every point (a very small hhh makes all weights underflow): for instance subtract the smallest squared distance before exponentiating.

Exercise 4.9 ★★★ — Rescuing k-NN from irrelevant features. On Breast Cancer, append m=100m = 100m=100 and then m=1000m = 1000m=1000 columns of Gaussian noise as in Section 4.7.2. (a) Compare, on 15 splits, the test accuracy of 5-NN (standardized), of 5-NN preceded by SelectKBest(f_classif, k=30) inside the pipeline, and of logistic regression. (b) How many of the original 30 features are among the 30 selected, on average? (c) Repeat (a) with the selection done before the split, on the whole data set (the leak of Section 2.7), and comment on what you see.

Hint. make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SelectKBest(f_classif, k=30), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)); the selected columns are given by pipe[1].get_support(); the original features are the first 30 columns.

Exercise 4.10 ★★★ — Consistency and the curse together. The world is: two equally likely classes, x∣y∼N(μy,Id)\mathbf{x} \mid y \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\mu_y, \mathbf{I}_d)x∣y∼N(μy​,Id​), with μ0=0\boldsymbol\mu_0 = \mathbf{0}μ0​=0 and μ1=(2,0,…,0)⊤\boldsymbol\mu_1 = (2, 0, \dots, 0)^\topμ1​=(2,0,…,0)⊤: only the first coordinate carries information, so the Bayes risk is Φ(−1)=0.1587\Phi(-1) = 0.1587Φ(−1)=0.1587 in every dimension ddd. (a) For d=2d = 2d=2 and d=10d = 10d=10, train k-NN with k≈nk \approx \sqrt{n}k≈n​ and with k≈n2/3k \approx n^{2/3}k≈n2/3 (odd), for n=30,100,300,1000,3000,10000n = 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000n=30,100,300,1000,3000,10000, and estimate the test error on 20,000 fresh points (6 repetitions). (b) Plot the errors against nnn with the Bayes risk. (c) For each ddd find the smallest nnn in the grid for which the error is within 0.01 of the Bayes risk, and relate the result to Section 4.7.

Hint. Reuse the structure of the experiment of Section 4.6.2; draw X = rng.normal(size=(n, d)); X[:, 0] += 2 * y.

What comes next¶

We have studied one method in depth, and the main lesson is general: every learning method has a knob that trades bias for variance, and the knob must be set with data it has not seen. Chapter 5 is devoted to that: validation sets, cross-validation, nested cross-validation, tuning hyperparameters systematically, and the metrics (precision, recall, ROC curves) that tell whether a classifier is good for the purpose at hand. Chapter 6 introduces the opposite assumption to k-NN: a global parametric model, the linear one, together with its regularization (ridge, regularized logistic regression), which is another knob of the same kind, whose bias and variance we shall analyze with the tools of this chapter. The kernel smoother of Exercise 4.8 anticipates the kernels of Chapter 9; the irrelevant features of Section 4.7.2 return in the feature selection and the sparse models of Chapter 10; decision trees (Chapter 11) are also local averages, but with neighborhoods that adapt to the data and ignore irrelevant features; and the intrinsic dimension of Section 4.7.3 will be made precise by PCA in Chapter 13.
